Mr. Stevens has lost water from his body through sweat. This loss of water leads to a contraction in the extracellular fluid volume and contraction of plasma volume. However, the RBC count is still the same as Mr. Stevens hasn't lost any blood. The same amount of RBCs in a smaller volume of fluid produces a higher hematocrit. As the water levels in the interstitial fluid and plasma decrease, the concentration of solutes dissolved inside (osmolarity) will increase. The higher concentrations of solutes in plasma makes it hypertonic relative to the RBCs. Consequently, water will flow out of the cells and reduce their volume. This process will lead to a reduced MCV. However, the MCV reduction is not severe enough to be obvious visually in a blood smear.
The ECF osmolality would drop, and water would flow into the ICF. Lower ECF osmolality would cause cell volume to increase.
ECF osmolality will increase. Water will flow out of the ICF. Cell volume will shrink.
